newsitem.title: USA: Plans set for dealing with U.S. terror attacks.
newsitem.headline: Plans set for dealing with U.S. terror attacks.

text.p: U.S. officials spelled out plans and displayed sophisticated new equipment on Friday to help American cities deal with chemical or biological weapon strikes like the sarin gas attack on Tokyo's subway system in 1995 that killed at least 12 people and injured 5,000 others.

But Oklahoma City Fire Chief Gary Marrs who dealt with a car-bombing attack on a federal office building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people two years ago, said cities were no better prepared now for such devastating attacks than Oklahoma was then.
"All of this is good and we certainly applaud the efforts but we needed it yesterday," Marrs told a House of Representatives National Security subcommittee. "It hasn't hit the streets yet."

Assistant Defence Secretary Allen Holmes told the subcommittee that federal experts would begin training Denver police and firefighters next month on how to deal with such disasters. Officials in more than 20 other cities would be trained over the next two years.

The training ultimately of officials in 120 U.S. cities will be conducted under a new programme approved by Congress last year to improve U.S. ability to deal with attacks like the sarin gas attack by the Aum Shinrikyo, a Japanese religious cult, on Tokyo subways on March 20, 1995.

Holmes said American cities would have to buy their own equipment to deal with such attacks. He said in some cases federal agencies have been able to develop equipment at a price the cities said they could afford.

Equipment displayed around the hearing room included a $10,000 suit and helmet to protect against chemical and biological weapons and low-level explosions, and a $20,000 kit still being developed for identifying biological war agents at a disaster scene.
There was also a $5,000 kit for identifying chemical war agents and a $2,500 robotic device that can rip open a car or truck suspected of containing explosives.

Other equipment carrying no price tags included a kevlar tent that can suppress the explosive impact of a bomb, various protective masks and equipment that improves a dog's ability to sniff out explosives and drugs.
